title: Nakamura Beats Erdogmus En Route To London Live Finals
summary:
GM Hikaru Nakamura of Team Falcons won the first Round of 16 match in the Speed Chess Championship XI with a 12-8 score against 15-year-old GM Yagiz Erdogmus. Erdogmus won the bullet segment, which is normally Nakamura's specialty, but it wasn't enough to make up for the six-point gap Nakamura created in the blitz segments. Nakamura earned $6,500 and Erdogmus $1,625 by win percentage.

The next Round of 16 match, between GMs Denis Lazavik and Dmitry Andreikin, will be on Friday, November 20 at 12:00 p.m. ET / 18:00 CET / 10:30 p.m. IST.

5+1: Nakamura 4.5-2.5 Erdogmus

3+1: Nakamura 5.5-1.5 Erdogmus

1+1: Nakamura 2-4 Erdogmus

Nakamura advances to the Quarterfinals, where he will face the winner of GM Nihal Sarin vs. GM Hans Niemann. Asked which he'd prefer to face, he said, "I'd much rather play Hans... not to say Hans is a bad player or anything," and highlighted Nihal's strength in this speed chess format.

2026 Speed Chess Championship Bracket

Nakamura already leads the Champions Chess Tour leaderboard, which will determine 12 players who will play in the 2027 Esports World Cup.

Champions Chess Tour Leaderboard

(See full leaderboard.)

The Speed Chess Championship is one of three events that count toward the CCT leaderboard. The two other paths to qualification are the Titled Tuesday Grand Prix and next year's Chess.com Open. Last year's EWC champion, GM Magnus Carlsen, gets automatic entry.

Nakamura 12-8 Erdogmus

Our team gave Nakamura 96-4 odds of winning the match against the youngest 2700 in history, who played his first SCC, but it didn't mean the match was a walk in the park. Nakamura said, "Yagiz is the most talented junior in the world, so I knew it wasn't going to be easy. I think mostly what I did very well was I kept the game very tricky, very tactical until the very end." Nakamura was "just better in the clutch moments" when both players were on seconds.

Yagiz is the most talented junior in the world, so I knew it wasn't going to be easy.

—Hikaru Nakamura

In the 11th edition of the SCC, Nakamura and Carlsen have five titles apiece and will be vying to be the first player to earn six.

5+1: Nakamura 4.5-2.5 Erdogmus

Nakamura built up an insurmountable lead in the first two segments of the match. In the 5+1 games, he took a two-point lead after winning four games and losing two, with just one draw.

More often than not, Nakamura built significant advantages on the clock, which allowed him to win even with outrageous disadvantages, like being down a rook. He also identified a weakness for his opponent: "He was a little too set in his openings." The Turkish star stuck with the same opening systems throughout the match, and it evidently backfired.

Nakamura took an early two-point lead, first winning on time in game two after Erdogmus found a brilliant defensive queen sacrifice. In game three, with three seconds against 30, Erdogmus (with Black) had no time to see that Nakamura's back rank was just as weak as his.

In game four, however, Erdogmus struck back with his first win. This would establish a funny pattern: Erdogmus' first three wins came right before a break. The youngster mounted a ferocious attack, and Nakamura was resourceful enough to survive into an exchange-down endgame. But that was the end of the good news.

After the break, Nakamura won two more games and ended the segment on a loss. In game five, Nakamura came back from a piece-down endgame to win with three pawns against a bishop. Then, he won from a rook-down position when Erdogmus didn't realize, after 43...Qf4+, it's already time to pull the brakes and repeat moves.

Erdogmus won the last game, swinging back from a lost position himself. Nakamura had a winning attack with a queen and two knights, but with little time, he hung one of them and laughed out loud as he resigned.

Hikaru had a winning attack, but he hangs his knight and laughs as he resigns the last game of the 5+1 segment! https://t.co/hykSpGKz6I #SpeedChess https://t.co/FSGxTDPVDz

— chess24 (@chess24com) November 16, 2026

3+1: Nakamura 5.5-1.5 Erdogmus

This was Nakamura's strongest segment, which he won with a four-point margin. Just as in the previous segment, game one was a draw and Nakamura won the next two.

The second consecutive win is our Game of the Day, a strategic game that the five-time champion won on the black side of the Queen's Gambit Declined. GM Rafael Leitao goes over it below.

True to the pattern, Erdogmus won the last game before the break, in an endgame with two minor pieces and a rook for the queen. But right after the break, Nakamura won another nice game on the black side of the Queen's Gambit Declined. Rather than promote his pawn to a queen, which would win a rook, he found the beautiful and unusual 43...Ng1 checkmate.

Nakamura went on to win two more games before the end of the segment, reaching the bullet segment with a six-point lead.

1+1: Nakamura 2-4 Erdogmus

The bullet segment was Erdogmus' best, but he was only able to put a two-point dent in Nakamura's lead. It helped Nakamura that he was able to drain nearly half the match clock in the first two games, which ended in long-winded draws.

After the two draws, Erdogmus won two games back to back. The first of those wins was a cautionary tale to any reader to think twice before touching that f-pawn, which can sometimes lead to disaster on the g1-a7 diagonal. Look how that played out:

In the next game, Nakamura called Erdogmus' bluff and picked up a free piece. The e-file wasn't so threatening after all!

Erdogmus won the last game of the match, but it was little consolation with regard to the overall match. Still, it had significance for the split of prize money by win percentage.

For Nakamura's fans, it was a powerful showing, but the matches will get tougher with every stage. Asked to pick a dark horse to win the event, he went with GM Sina Movahed, who faces Carlsen on December 16—that is, if he had to pick a dark horse. Nakamura pointed out that Movahed probably should have beaten Lazavik in the Esports World Cup last year and has great potential in speed chess. We'll see!

Speaking of Lazavik, he plays the next SCC match this Friday.

How to watch?

You can watch the event on Chess.com/TV or on GM Hikaru Nakamura's Kick channel. You can also enjoy the show on our Twitch and catch all our live broadcasts on YouTube.com/Chess. Games from the event can be viewed on our events page.

The live broadcast was hosted by GMs Aman Hambleton and Robert Hess.

The Speed Chess Championship, which starts on November 16 and culminates with Live Finals on February 7, 2027 in London, is Chess.com's most important speed chess event. Some of the biggest names in chess compete to determine the best speed chess player in the world. The games are played with time controls of 5+1, 3+1, and 1+1. The prize fund is $250,000.

title: JP Morgan Chase Wins North American Corporate Chess League Season 14
summary:
JP Morgan Chase won the 14th season of the North American Corporate Chess League in an exciting final match against PWC, taking the title 3-2. It was the banking company's first championship. The company fielded a strong team led by IM Edward Song, FMs Alex Bian and Maggie Feng, NM Asuka Nakamura (brother of GM Hikaru Nakamura), and Calvin Yang.

You can see coverage of the knockout matches, hosted by GM Kayden Troff, below.

Quarterfinals

A successful regular season earned JP Morgan Chase the top seed entering the knockout phase. In the quarterfinals they faced the tech company NVIDIA, led by IM Bogdan-Gabriel Vioreanu. Song faced technical issues to start the playoffs and forfeited his game against Vioreanu. That was the only victory for NVIDIA, while Yang and Nakamura scored for JP Morgan Chase to take a tight match, 3-2.

Semifinals

In the semifinals, JP Morgan Chase faced Susquehanna, who had defeated the defending champions, Jane Street, in the previous round. Nakamura led the way again with a critical victory, while Bian defeated Brian Luo in a sharp game.

Nicolas Brinkman struck back for Susquehanna by defeating Yang, but it wasn't enough. JP Morgan Chase advanced 3-2, earning a spot in the finals.

Finals

PWC was led by GM Andrey Baryshpolets, and they defeated Meta to earn a finals matchup against JP Morgan Chase. Baryshpolets defeated Song in a complicated game, and PWC's Mark Morrison moved to 3/3 on the day by defeating Yang. JP Morgan Chase struck on the other boards. Nakamura won his third game of the day, defeating NM David Siamon. Bian defeated Michael Giampa and Feng defeated Alexander Fogel in a tricky endgame.

Feng's victory clinched the title for JP Morgan Chase, winning the match 3-2 and bringing the company its first title in the 14-year history of the league.

The North American Corporate Chess League brings together companies headquartered in the U.S., Canada, and Mexico for seven weeks of team chess competition on Chess.com.

title: Here Comes The SCC: Who's Playing, Who Will Win In Round 1
summary:
Speed Chess Championship XI is almost here. Which of its 16 players will win all four of their matches, earn the biggest share of $250,000, and take home the most Champions Chess Tour (CCT) standings points on their way to the 2027 Esports World Cup?

Perhaps nothing matters more for a player entering the first round than their opponent. In this year's SCC, who's playing whom, and who are the statistical favorites? Let's find out! Thanks to NM Jeremy Kane for running the prediction numbers.

Hikaru Nakamura vs. Yagiz Erdogmus

Magnus Carlsen vs. Sina Movahed

Alireza Firouzja vs. Vladislav Artemiev

Denis Lazavik vs. Dmitry Andreikin

Wesley So vs. Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu

Nihal Sarin vs. Hans Niemann

Nodirbek Abdusattorov vs. Vincent Keymer

Fabiano Caruana vs. Javokhir Sindarov

Hikaru Nakamura vs. Yagiz Erdogmus

The tournament begins November 16 in a match between the player tied for the most SCC victories with five, GM Hikaru Nakamura, and the youngest player in the field, 15-year-old GM Yagiz Erdogmus.

Match Prediction

Erdogmus has a steep uphill climb, but the task is not completely insurmountable.

Player | Odds of Winning | Predicted Score

Hikaru Nakamura | 96% | 16.5

Yagiz Kaan Erdogmus | 4% | 7.5

Magnus Carlsen vs. Sina Movahed

A common theme in this year's first round is 30-somethings playing teenagers. This is also the first match by seeding, with GM Magnus Carlsen the heavy favorite against GM Sina Movahed, but Movahed is just the type of player the SCC is built for. Like Carlsen, he has won three Titled Tuesdays in 2026, more than all but one other player. Movahed is the second-youngest player in the field and, despite his seeding, very dangerous.

Match Prediction

Like Erdogmus, Movahed has a tough task, but he knows that. It's Magnus Carlsen, after all. Still, about one times in 11, the youngster scores the major upset.

Player | Odds of Winning | Predicted Score

Magnus Carlsen | 91% | 14.5

Sina Movahed | 9% | 9.5

Alireza Firouzja vs. Vladislav Artemiev

GM Vladislav Artemiev is just 28, but it feels like he has been around a long time. The same can also be said for his first-round opponent, GM Alireza Firouzja, still just 23.

Match Prediction

The numbers show a big edge for Firouzja, even larger than Carlsen's over Movahed. Subjectively speaking, while Firouzja seems like the favorite, Artemiev's odds also seem better than this.

Player | Odds of Winning | Predicted Score

Alireza Firouzja | 93% | 15.5

Vladislav Artemiev | 7% | 8.5

Denis Lazavik vs. Dmitry Andreikin

Nakamura–Erdogmus and Carlsen–Movahed aren't the only Vet vs. Youngster matchups, although GM Denis Lazavik is now himself a 19-year-old veteran of the SCC and EWC alike. His opponent, GM Dmitry Andreikin, however, is one of the original online chess stars, who still has more Titled Tuesday victories than almost anyone.

Match Prediction

No shocker here that the 2026 EWC finalist Lazavik wins about five times in seven, but that is still a good chance for Andreikin.

Player | Odds of Winning | Predicted Score

Denis Lazavik | 71% | 13.5

Dmitry Andreikin | 29% | 10.5

Wesley So vs. Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu

GM Wesley So had quite a 2026, winning multiple tournaments and starring in Grandmasters. He faces GM Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu, who at 21 years old has already played in multiple Candidates Tournaments. At age 33 against 21, it's another generational matchup. (The 12-letter difference in a So–Praggnanandhaa match is a coincidence.)

Match Prediction

A pretty close match here, Praggnanandhaa winning about three times in five.

Player | Odds of Winning | Predicted Score

Wesley So | 39% | 11.0

Praggnanandhaa R | 61% | 13.0

Nihal Sarin vs. Hans Niemann

This is one match that proves that speed chess is a young person's game. GM Nihal Sarin faces off against GM Hans Niemann in the only first-round matchup where the players' names start with the same syllable (Nihal vs. Niemann).

Match Prediction

Nihal wins about two-thirds of the time, but if there's anything we know about Niemann, it's that he won't go quietly.

Player | Odds of Winning | Predicted Score

Nihal Sarin | 68% | 13.5

Hans Niemann | 32% | 10.5

Nodirbek Abdusattorov vs. Vincent Keymer

In another youthful matchup, GM Nodirbek Abdusattorov will take on GM Vincent Keymer in a battle of world top 10s, one of two such matchups in the first round. A decade from now, we could look back on this match as a precursor to a world championship match. For now, it's just two incandescent young stars battling it out.

Match Prediction

While this feels like a pure coin flip, Abdusattorov wins more often than not.

Player | Odds of Winning | Predicted Score

Nodirbek Abdusattorov | 58% | 12.5

Vincent Keymer | 42% | 11.5

Fabiano Caruana vs. Javokhir Sindarov

And this is the other matchup between current top 10s. GM Javokhir Sindarov will be spending the end of November and start of December trying to win the Salesforce FIDE World Championship. Whether he's the freshly minted world champ or not by the time of his SCC match, Sindarov will be a big challenge for GM Fabiano Caruana in another match between two players on different sides of age 30.

Match Prediction

No surprise, this is the closest match by the numbers, even closer to a pure coin flip than Abdusattorov–Keymer.

Player | Odds of Winning | Predicted Score

Fabiano Caruana | 47% | 11.5

Javokhir Sindarov | 53% | 12.5

Conclusion

And that's the first round, with several exciting matches that will pit experience against exuberance. From there, the eight winners will become four in the quarterfinals, before heading to London in February for the dramatic semis and finals.

See our SCC events page for all the broadcast details, and tune in throughout!

title: Meet The 7-Year-Old Magnus Carlsen Who Dreams Of Becoming A Grandmaster
summary:
When Bernard Sanico&rsquo;s son was born in 2019, he knew exactly what to call him. A fan of the world champion since he was 12, he named the boy Magnus Carlsen Sanico. Seven years later, the younger Magnus is a rising player in the Philippines dr...

When Bernard Sanico’s son was born in 2019, he knew exactly what to call him. A fan of the world champion since he was 12, he named the boy Magnus Carlsen Sanico. Seven years later, the younger Magnus is a rising player in the Philippines dreaming of becoming a grandmaster.

The original GM Magnus Carlsen, perhaps the greatest chess player of all time, has inspired fans globally to pick up the game. One of them is a Filipino father who became a fan of the Norwegian in 2009.

"We made a deal. If the baby is a boy, I'll decide the name. If it's a girl, the mother decides," he told Chess.com. "The real reason is I am the number one fan of the greatest Magnus Carlsen," he said.

We made a deal. If the baby is a boy, I'll decide the name. If it's a girl, the mother decides

—Bernard Sanico

The result: Magnus Carlsen Sanico.

Magnus Carlsen Sanico. Photo: Bernard Sanico.

Bernard said the family had no issues with his choice, although an explanation behind the choice was sometimes necessary. His son has known who he was named after since daycare.

29-year-old Bernard teaches beginners in their hometown of Kolambugan, in Lanao del Norte on the southern Philippine island of Mindanao. He plays only online himself, where he is rated around 2000, and Bernard would take Magnus along as he introduced other children to chess.

In March 2025, when he was five, Magnus decided he wanted to learn the game. "Dad, teach me also chess," Bernard recalled him saying. He noted that the interest came from his son, and sharing a name with the five-time world champion had never meant that Magnus had to become a chess player.

Now, around 20 months later, Sanico estimates his son has played around 35 tournaments, mostly local events, plus some national ones. "He puts extra pressure on his opponents because of the name," Bernard joked.

He puts extra pressure on his opponents because of the name.

—Bernard Sanico

Magnus Carlsen Sanico with his father. Photo: Benard Sanico.

At the ASEAN Youth U10 Boys Championship in Misamis Occidental on November 7–9, Magnus scored 4.5/7 and finished 10th, competing against older children in the under-10 section.

He then joined a field of grandmasters and international masters at the Misamis Occidental Philippines International Chess Championship, which concluded on November 16. His 4/9, scoring three wins and two draws, was an impressive result for a seven-year-old.

He held a draw against a 1930-rated opponent, and defeated two players rated 1516 and 1784.

Magnus Carlsen Sanico's performance in the Philippines.

Magnus already has published FIDE ratings of 1495 in rapid and 1755 in blitz, and is set to achieve a classical rating in the high 1600s on the next rating list. That will make him one of the world's highest rated players born in 2019 or later.

"He tells me that he really enjoys the experience and feels happy to compete in such a big tournament. He is excited to play against strong and experienced players, including national and international-level competitors," his father said.

"He is learning to be more confident, disciplined, and humble. We always remind him to enjoy the game."

Magnus Carlsen Sanico won his fourth round game in the Misamis Occidental Philippines International Chess Championship. Photo: Bernard Sanico.

Bernard told Chess.com that supporting the enthusiasm has required some sacrifices. He has been forced to change his working life, giving up a steady job away from home to focus on Magnus. He now earns money by helping in his uncle's furniture business.

Father and son train every day, but Bernard says his own knowledge is limited and he cannot afford a separate coach.

In the Filipino chess community, Magnus Carlsen Sanico has generated some attention, helped by some media coverage and a Facebook page with nearly 7000 followers.

With travels being a significant expense, Bernard says Magnus' elementary school and a community official helped contribute toward the trip to the Misamis Occidental tournament, two hours from their home. A business sponsored the family's accommodation at the resort.

Magnus Carlsen Sanico with an impressive performance in his first major international tournament. Photo: Bernard Sanico.

Outside chess, his father said Magnus enjoys school, does well in math, and likes hiking. In chess, however, his ambition is clear. He wants to play more tournaments and become a grandmaster.

When Chess.com asked Bernard what his own dream is, his answer was clear: "My dream is what Magnus dreams for himself. I just support him."

My dream is what Magnus dreams for himself. I just support him.

—Bernard Sanico
